newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina's YPF says briefly postponing share sale.
newsitem.headline: Argentina's YPF says briefly postponing share sale.

text.p: Argentine oil company YPF said Tuesday the sale of 10 percent of its shares was briefly postponed after a judge blocked the deal.
"It was decided yesterday to briefly postpone the sale of the shares," the company told the Buenos Aires Stock Exchange in a statement.
The block of shares are held by employees.

"At the request of certain employees who left YPF before its privatization in July 7, 1993, a judge took preemptive measures that banned any transaction on the 10 percent of the YPF shares under the Shared Property Program," YPF said.
The company said it was analyzing the ruling by a labor judge Monday.
It added it was seeking a short-term solution to the situation. It did not elaborate.
A source close to the deal said the delay was not expected to last more than a few days.
He added that the bids, both local and international, were very satisfactory and another source stressed that nobody withdrew their bids after the suspension was announced.
Earlier Tuesday, the proxy for YPF's employees said the employees and the Argentine state would challenge the judge's ruling.
"The ruling is an aberration," Pablo Grigio Campana, proxy for YPF's 4,673 employees in the deal, told Reuters.
"It is a strange decision upholding a claim by 11 former YPF's employees who did not even have the right to participate in the program as they left the company before it was implemented."
The cut-off price for the auction of the YPF shares should have been announced at 1015 local time/1315 GMT Tuesday.

Banco Comafi and Merchant Bankers Asociados, an Argentine affiliate of Salomon Brothers Inc as well as Salomon Brothers in New York, has been accepting bids for the shares since 1700 local time Monday.
Argentina's government authorized the sale of the 33.5 million Class C YPF shares in the hands of the company's employees --10 percent of the firm's stock -- by a decree issued last Friday.
The government owns another 20 percent of the firm but says it has no immediate plans to sell.
Proceeds from the sale are expected to slightly exceed $1.0 billion. From that amount, employees owe the government $650 million.
